title: How great leaders inspire action
speaker: Simon Sinek
notice: The whole talk hangs on one simple model (why, how, what), stated early and returned to again and again.

title: The danger of a single story
speaker: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
notice: Short personal stories each build towards one idea, and the key phrase returns deliberately rather than by accident.

title: The best stats you've ever seen
speaker: Hans Rosling
notice: Complex data explained in plain words, one change at a time, with the listener told exactly what to look at.

title: How to speak so that people want to listen
speaker: Julian Treasure
notice: He talks about pace, pitch, volume and silence while demonstrating each one. Listen to how he uses pauses.

title: Grit: the power of passion and perseverance
speaker: Angela Lee Duckworth
notice: A short talk that states its finding plainly and early, then explains it without padding.

title: Try something new for 30 days
speaker: Matt Cutts
notice: About three minutes: one idea, short sentences, and a clear challenge to the audience at the end.

title: How to start a movement
speaker: Derek Sivers
notice: He explains an idea by narrating a single example step by step, then states the lesson in one line.

title: Do schools kill creativity?
speaker: Sir Ken Robinson
notice: A relaxed, conversational pace; the stories and humour all serve one argument he keeps coming back to.

title: The puzzle of motivation
speaker: Dan Pink
notice: He sets out his case like a lawyer: claim, evidence, and clear signposts as he moves from one point to the next.

title: The power of introverts
speaker: Susan Cain
notice: One argument developed through a personal story, then research, ending with specific calls to action.

title: Inside the mind of a master procrastinator
speaker: Tim Urban
notice: An abstract idea made concrete with simple characters and everyday examples.

title: The power of vulnerability
speaker: Brené Brown
notice: Research presented as a personal story, with natural pauses that let key moments land.

title: TED's secret to great public speaking
speaker: Chris Anderson
notice: Practical advice on building one idea in a listener's mind, step by step, in plain language.

title: How I harnessed the wind
speaker: William Kamkwamba
notice: A simple, chronological story told in short, plain sentences. Clarity doesn't need complicated words.

title: Inaugural address (1961)
speaker: John F. Kennedy
notice: Balanced, contrasting sentences and deliberate pauses that give key lines room to land.

title: We shall fight on the beaches (1940)
speaker: Winston Churchill
notice: A repeated opening phrase builds intensity towards the close: repetition used on purpose, not by accident.

title: Stanford commencement address (2005)
speaker: Steve Jobs
notice: He announces the structure at the start (three stories) and signposts each one as he goes.

title: Remarks at the Brandenburg Gate (1987)
speaker: Ronald Reagan
notice: The argument builds towards one short, direct demand, delivered with emphasis and space around it.

title: Nobel lecture (2004)
speaker: Wangari Maathai
notice: A personal story of starting small (planting trees) that widens into a larger message and a clear closing.
